```{r}
# Install if needed: install.packages(c("tidyverse", "readxl"))
library(tidyverse)
library(readxl)
```

```{r}
# Q1a: Describe the data
print("Structure of the mpg dataset:")
str(mpg)
print("\nSummary of the mpg dataset:")
summary(mpg)
```

```{r}
# Q1b: Plot the number of cars per model using geom_bar()
# Use fct_reorder to sort the bars by count for better visualization
mpg %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = fct_reorder(model, model, .fun = length))) +
  geom_bar(fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(
    title = "Number of Cars per Model in the MPG Dataset",
    x = "Model",
    y = "Number of Cars"
  ) +
  coord_flip() + # Flip coordinates for readability
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
#Continuous Variables (Numeric): displ (engine displacement), year (often treated as categorical/integer, but numerically continuous), cyl (number of cylinders, often treated as discrete/categorical), cty (city MPG), hwy (highway MPG).

#Categorical Variables (Character/Factor): manufacturer, model, trans (transmission type), drv (drive train), fl (fuel type), class (type of car).

#Continuous Variable for Q1d/Q1e: displ (engine displacement) is a suitable continuous variable for mapping to a scatter plot aesthetic.
```

```{r}
# Q1d: Plot cty vs hwy. Color mapped by class.
ggplot(mpg, aes(x = cty, y = hwy, color = class)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  labs(
    title = "City vs. Highway Mileage by Vehicle Class",
    x = "City Miles Per Gallon (cty)",
    y = "Highway Miles Per Gallon (hwy)",
    color = "Car Class"
  ) +
  theme_bw()
```

```{r}
# Q1e: Plot displ vs hwy. Color mapped by drv.
ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy, color = drv)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  labs(
    title = "Engine Displacement vs. Highway Mileage by Drive Train",
    x = "Engine Displacement (liters)",
    y = "Highway Miles Per Gallon (hwy)",
    color = "Drive Train (drv)"
  ) +
  theme_classic()
```

```{r}
# Q2a: Import the traffic.csv file
df_traffic <- read_csv("traffic.csv")

# Get number of observations (rows) and variables (columns)
cat("Number of Observations (Rows):", nrow(df_traffic), "\n")
cat("Number of Variables (Columns):", ncol(df_traffic), "\n")
cat("Variables and their types (using str):\n")
str(df_traffic)
```

```{r}
# Q2b: Subset the traffic dataset into separate data frames for each unique junction

# Assuming 'Junction' is a categorical column in df_traffic
junctions_list <- split(df_traffic, df_traffic$Junction)

# Display the first few rows of the data for Junction 1 (as an example result)
print("Subsetted data for Junction 1 (Head):")
head(junctions_list[[1]])
```

```{r}
# Q2c: Plot each junction in a using geom_line()
# This requires a date/time variable on the x-axis and traffic count on the y-axis.
# Assuming x-axis = DateTime, y-axis = Vehicles.

ggplot(df_traffic, aes(x = DateTime, y = Vehicles, color = as.factor(Junction))) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(
    title = "Traffic Flow Over Time by Junction",
    x = "Date and Time",
    y = "Vehicle Count",
    color = "Junction ID"
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~Junction, scales = "free_y", ncol = 1) + # Plot each junction in its own panel
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
# Q3a: Import alexa_file.xlsx (assuming Sheet1)
df_alexa <- read_excel("alexa_file.xlsx")

# Get info
cat("Number of Observations (Rows):", nrow(df_alexa), "\n")
cat("Number of Columns (Variables):", ncol(df_alexa), "\n")
cat("Variables and their types (using str):\n")
str(df_alexa)
```

```{r}
# Q3b: Group variations and get the total count using dplyr
variation_counts <- df_alexa %>%
  group_by(variation) %>%
  summarise(Total_Reviews = n(), .groups = 'drop')

print("Total Count of Reviews per Variation:")
variation_counts
```

```{r}
# Q3c: Plot the variation counts
variation_counts %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = fct_reorder(variation, Total_Reviews), y = Total_Reviews)) +
  geom_col(fill = "darkgreen") +
  labs(
    title = "Total Number of Reviews by Alexa Product Variation",
    x = "Product Variation",
    y = "Total Number of Reviews (Count)"
  ) +
  coord_flip() + # Flip for better label readability
  theme_bw()
```

```{r}
# Q3d: Plot geom_line() with date and number of verified reviews
# Requires aggregating the total number of verified reviews per date.
df_alexa %>%
  group_by(date) %>%
  summarise(Total_Verified_Reviews = sum(verified_reviews, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = 'drop') %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = date, y = Total_Verified_Reviews)) +
  geom_line(color = "red") +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE) + # Optional: add a trend line
  labs(
    title = "Trend of Total Verified Reviews Over Time",
    x = "Date",
    y = "Total Verified Reviews (Count)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
# Q3e: Get the relationship of variations and ratings.

# Find the mean rating for each variation
variation_ratings <- df_alexa %>%
  group_by(variation) %>%
  summarise(
    Mean_Rating = mean(rating, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = 'drop'
  ) %>%
  # Find which variation has the highest mean rating
  arrange(desc(Mean_Rating))

print("Mean Rating by Variation:")
print(variation_ratings)
cat("\nVariation with the highest mean rating:", variation_ratings$variation[1])

# Plot the relationship using a column chart
variation_ratings %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = fct_reorder(variation, Mean_Rating), y = Mean_Rating)) +
  geom_col(fill = "purple") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Average Rating by Alexa Product Variation",
    x = "Product Variation",
    y = "Mean Rating (1-5)"
  ) +
  theme_bw()
```
